correctness.rationale: Cusick’s fourth-power recurrence has \(H_0=1\), \(H_1=2\). Subtraction gives \(W_n=-4n(4n-1)(4n+1)W_{n-1}/(n+1)^3\), hence an exact product. At \(n=p-1\) for every prime \(p\ge5\), the linear factors \(4j\pm1\) have exactly two distinct roots among \(1,\ldots,p-1\) and are strictly smaller than \(p^2\), so the numerator \(p\)-valuation is exactly two, while \((p!)^3\) has valuation three. Therefore \(\nu_p(W_{p-1})=\nu_p(v-2u)-1\) for nonzero discrepancy. Integrality of both adjacent \(U\) values contradicts this if \(p\) does not divide the discrepancy. Every nonzero integer has infinitely many nondividing primes. Zero discrepancy yields integer multiples of \(H\) by initial-value uniqueness. Tested using exact rationals in 672 determinant instances and 22 primes; finite checks are not the infinite proof.

value.rationale: The question classifies all integer initial values for a natural, classical second-order polynomial recurrence whose canonical binomial-sum solution is integral. It answers the complete integral lattice problem and gives a sharp, parameter-uniform obstruction at every \(p\ge5\) not dividing the initial discrepancy, rather than a finite example or routine recomputation. The local two-root arithmetic is special to the fourth-power recurrence and distinguishes it from cubic Franel results.
